title: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration
summary: Describes how an IPv6 host configures its own interface addresses. It generates a link-local address, builds global addresses from router-advertised prefixes, and runs Duplicate Address Detection to check that no one else on the link is using the same address. It is a draft standard.

eli5.summary: A computer can give itself an address without asking a boss. It makes up a name tag from what it knows, then checks that no one else wears the same one.

questions: what is a link-local address in ipv6
what is the difference between slaac and dhcpv6
subtitle: How an IPv6 host gives itself an address with no manual setup and no server, then checks that nobody else is using it.

tldr.problem: IPv6 hosts need unique addresses on every link, and requiring manual setup or a DHCPv6 server for every machine would make small and large networks harder to run.
tldr.mechanism: A host builds a link-local address from the well-known prefix and an interface identifier, checks it with Duplicate Address Detection, then combines prefixes from Router Advertisements with its interface identifier to form global addresses.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2462 and has since been updated by RFC 7527 and RFC 9762. The method is not completely reliable, and stateless autoconfiguration can be used together with DHCPv6.

today: RFC 4862 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2462 and is updated by RFC 7527 and RFC 9762. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What Stateless Autoconfiguration Is
sections.content:
RFC 4862 specifies the steps an IPv6 host takes to autoconfigure its interfaces. The process has three parts: generating a link-local address, generating global addresses through stateless address autoconfiguration, and the Duplicate Address Detection procedure that verifies an address is unique on the link.

The stateless mechanism needs no manual configuration of hosts, minimal (if any) configuration of routers, and no additional servers. Routers advertise prefixes that identify the subnets on a link. The host generates an interface identifier that identifies its interface on that subnet. The address is the two combined.

The stateless approach suits sites that do not care about the exact addresses hosts use, so long as they are unique and routable. Sites that want tighter control over assignments use DHCPv6, and both may be used at the same time. The process applies to hosts, not routers, although routers are expected to form link-local addresses this way and to pass Duplicate Address Detection on all their addresses.
sections.eli5: Instead of waiting for someone to hand out house numbers, each computer builds its own from its street name and something that belongs only to it. Then it checks the number is not taken.

sections.title: Design Goals and Address Leasing
sections.content:
The RFC lists four goals. Machines should not need manual configuration before joining a network. Small sites with one link should not need a DHCPv6 server or a router to communicate, which link-local addresses make possible. Large sites with many networks and routers should not need a DHCPv6 server for addresses either, because routers periodically advertise the active prefixes on a link. Finally, configuration should make site renumbering graceful.

Renumbering works because addresses are leased to an interface for a fixed, possibly infinite, time. Each address has a preferred lifetime and a valid lifetime. After the preferred lifetime the address is deprecated, and after the valid lifetime it is invalid. An interface can hold several addresses, so a new address and the one being phased out can work side by side during a transition.

TCP provides no support for changing end-point addresses mid-connection, so an address that becomes invalid breaks open connections. For that reason the deprecation period should be long enough that most communications have moved to the new address by the time the old one becomes invalid.
sections.eli5: Addresses are like library books on loan: they have a due date. Before the due date the computer stops starting new things with the old address, so everything can switch to the new one in time.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
Autoconfiguration is performed only on multicast-capable links and starts when a multicast-capable interface is enabled, for example at system startup. Nodes first generate a link-local address, which is the well-known link-local prefix with an identifier of the interface appended. The node tests this tentative address before using it. If it is not unique, autoconfiguration stops and manual configuration is required. If it is unique, the node has IP-level connectivity with its neighbors.

The remaining steps are for hosts only. A host sends one or more Router Solicitations to the all-routers multicast group to get a Router Advertisement quickly instead of waiting for the next periodic one. Advertisements carry Prefix Information options. The autonomous address-configuration flag says whether an option applies to stateless autoconfiguration, and other fields give a subnet prefix with preferred and valid lifetimes.

By default all addresses should be tested for uniqueness before assignment, whether obtained manually, through stateless autoconfiguration or through DHCPv6. A per-interface flag can disable the test for sites that think its overhead outweighs its benefit. To save time, a host may generate and verify its link-local address in parallel with waiting for a Router Advertisement.
sections.eli5: First the computer makes a name tag that works on its own street and checks nobody has it. Then it asks the street's signpost which neighborhood it is in, and makes a longer address that works everywhere.

sections.title: Forming Link-Local and Global Addresses
sections.content:
A link-local address is built from the well-known prefix FE80::0. The left-most prefix-length bits are the prefix, the bits to the right are set to zeroes, and the right-most N bits, where N is the interface identifier length, are replaced by the interface identifier. If the prefix length plus N is larger than 128, autoconfiguration fails and manual configuration is required. A link-local address has an infinite preferred and valid lifetime and is never timed out.

Global addresses are formed from the prefix in a Prefix Information option plus an interface identifier. If the prefix length and the identifier length do not add up to 128 bits, the option MUST be ignored. The RFC does not hard-code an identifier length. It is set by the link-type specific document and the address architecture, and implementations should expect any length.

Creation of global addresses SHOULD be locally configurable, but the processing MUST be enabled by default.
sections.eli5: An address is two pieces glued together: the street part that routers announce, and the house part that belongs to the computer. If the two pieces do not fit, the computer throws the announcement away.

sections.title: Duplicate Address Detection
sections.content:
Duplicate Address Detection MUST be performed on all unicast addresses before they are assigned to an interface, however they were obtained. It MUST NOT be performed on anycast addresses. Each individual unicast address SHOULD be tested. Skipping the test for a global address that shares an interface identifier with the link-local address is NOT RECOMMENDED, and new implementations MUST NOT do it, because addresses with different identifiers now exist, such as those from RFC 4941.

The test uses Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement messages. The node sends DupAddrDetectTransmits solicitations, spaced RetransTimer milliseconds apart. The Target Address is the address being checked, the IP source is the unspecified address, and the IP destination is the solicited-node multicast address of the target. Before sending, the interface MUST join the all-nodes multicast address and the solicited-node multicast address of the tentative address. A node SHOULD delay joining by a random time between 0 and MAX_RTR_SOLICITATION_DELAY when it is the first message after initialization, to ease congestion when many nodes start together.

The address is a duplicate if a solicitation for it arrives from another node, or if a Neighbor Advertisement for it arrives. A node MUST NOT respond to a Neighbor Solicitation for a tentative address. If no test shows a duplicate within RetransTimer milliseconds after the last solicitation, the address is unique and may be assigned.

A duplicate MUST NOT be assigned, and the node SHOULD log a system management error. If the duplicate link-local address came from a hardware-based identifier, IP operation on the interface SHOULD be disabled. The RFC also admits the method is not completely reliable, for example if the link was partitioned while it ran.
sections.eli5: Before keeping a new name tag, the computer shouts, "Is anyone already called this?" If anyone answers, or shouts the same name at the same time, it must pick a different one.

sections.title: Processing Router Advertisements
sections.content:
For each Prefix Information option in a Router Advertisement the host applies rules in order. It silently ignores the option if the Autonomous flag is not set, if the prefix is the link-local prefix, or if the preferred lifetime is greater than the valid lifetime. Otherwise, if the prefix is new and the valid lifetime is not 0, it forms an address and adds it to its list with the lifetimes from the option.

If the prefix matches an existing autoconfigured address, the preferred lifetime is reset to the advertised value. The valid lifetime follows a protective rule. If the advertised valid lifetime is greater than 2 hours or greater than the remaining lifetime, it is accepted. If the remaining lifetime is 2 hours or less, the option is ignored for the valid lifetime unless the advertisement was authenticated, for example with Secure Neighbor Discovery (RFC 3971). Otherwise the valid lifetime is reset to 2 hours.

These rules block a denial-of-service attack in which a bogus advertisement carries very small valid lifetimes and makes all of a node's addresses expire early. Legitimate periodic advertisements cancel the short lifetimes before they take effect. Preferred lifetimes are not protected this way because that attack is relatively minor and administrators legitimately use short ones to deprecate an address.

A link counts as having no routers if no advertisements arrive after a small number of solicitations. DHCPv6 may still be available then. A forwarding node that does not send advertisements has to be configured manually as the default router, because advertisements are the only automatic way to learn it.
sections.eli5: When the signpost announces a neighborhood, the computer checks the announcement makes sense. It does not let one sneaky note shrink its address's life to nearly nothing, because real signposts keep repeating the true message.

sections.title: Address Lifetimes and Expiry
sections.content:
An address is tentative until Duplicate Address Detection succeeds. It then becomes preferred, meaning its use is unrestricted. When the preferred lifetime expires it becomes deprecated, and when the valid lifetime expires it becomes invalid. Valid addresses are preferred or deprecated, and the valid lifetime must be greater than or equal to the preferred lifetime.

A deprecated address SHOULD continue to be used as a source address in existing communications but SHOULD NOT start new ones if another non-deprecated address of sufficient scope can easily be used. IP and higher layers MUST still accept and process datagrams sent to a deprecated address. For TCP, a SYN sent to a deprecated address is answered with a SYN-ACK from that same address if the connection would otherwise be allowed.

An invalid address MUST NOT be used as a source address in outgoing communications and MUST NOT be recognized as a destination on a receiving interface.
sections.eli5: An address goes from brand new, to still fine but being retired, to not usable at all. While it is being retired, old conversations may keep using it but new ones should pick a fresh one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Stateless autoconfiguration lets a host connect, configure an address and start communicating without registering or authenticating with the local site. The RFC notes that this lets unauthorized users use a network, but says the threat is inherent in the Internet architecture, because any node physically attached to a network can generate an address that provides connectivity.

Autoconfiguration and Duplicate Address Detection also open up denial-of-service attacks. For example, any node can answer Neighbor Solicitations for a tentative address, which makes the other node reject the address as a duplicate. RFC 3756 discusses these attacks in detail, and they can be addressed with Secure Neighbor Discovery (RFC 3971). The RFC adds that IP security is not always feasible depending on the network environment.
sections.eli5: Anyone standing on the street can get an address, and a prankster can shout "that name is mine!" to stop a newcomer. There is a locked-down version of the shouting that stops the pranks.

messages.label: Neighbor Solicitation
messages.note: Target is the tentative address, source is the unspecified address, destination is its solicited-node multicast address.

messages.label: Neighbor Advertisement
messages.note: Sent only if another node already uses the address. If one arrives, the address is not unique.
